implementation_notes: Documents are ordinary Rust structs and serde owns the codec: #[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)] generates implementations at compile time (no runtime reflection), serde_json::to_vec/to_string writes the document and from_slice/from_str rebuilds it, with #[serde(rename)] pinning wire names, #[serde(default)] plus Option making fields optional and #[serde(tag = ...)] giving enum documents the discriminator the contract needs. Because serde is format-agnostic the same document type travels as JSON, CBOR or MessagePack unchanged, and that is what replaces the classic message class. Hand-written codecs remain justified for no_std targets or fixed binary layouts, and the schema-first alternative is the prost variant.
code_sketch:
#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]
#[serde(rename_all = "snake_case")]
pub struct OrderShipped {
    pub version: u8,
    pub order_id: String,
    pub lines: Vec<Line>,
}

let wire = serde_json::to_vec(&doc)?;                   // producer
match serde_json::from_slice::<OrderShipped>(&body) {   // receiver decides
    Ok(doc) => apply(doc),
    Err(e) => dead_letter(&body, e.to_string())?,
}
pitfalls: Serde ignores unknown fields and fails on missing ones: keep new fields optional with #[serde(default)] and Option or older consumers stop decoding.
Enum representations are not portable - the tagged/untagged choice must match the producer's other languages, and untagged enums report only 'data did not match any variant'.
serde_json has no automatic big-integer support beyond i64/u64, so 64-bit identifiers that exceed f64 precision must travel as strings.
Deserializing into borrowed &str fields needs explicit lifetimes and #[serde(borrow)]; requiring DeserializeOwned instead forces copies of every string.

variants.name: prost generated documents (protobuf)
variants.implementation_notes: prost generates plain Rust structs from .proto files: each message becomes a struct deriving prost::Message, scalar fields map to the obvious Rust types, oneofs become enums, and encoding and decoding go through the bytes::Buf/BufMut abstractions rather than std::io. Code is produced by prost-build in a build script and requires protoc (prost-build no longer bundles it), so the toolchain is part of the build; prost deliberately omits runtime reflection and descriptors, which keeps the generated types simple but leaves introspection to generated code. Choose it when the document contract is protobuf and shared with other languages; its current MSRV is 1.85.
pitfalls: protoc must be installed (with prost-build v0.11+ it is no longer bundled), so the build fails on machines that only have cargo.
Generated types live in OUT_DIR and are re-created on every clean build; vendoring them by hand breaks the version contract with prost itself.
prost has no reflection or descriptors, so generic tooling (schema registry introspection, dynamic routing by type) needs separate generated metadata.
